question: Using the current WHATWG URL Standard, which normalization steps are performed when parsing an HTTPS URL containing Unicode hostnames, default ports, dot segments, fragments, and percent-encoded path bytes?

claims.text: Parsing lowercases the scheme, so an uppercase HTTPS scheme such as `HTTPS:` becomes `https:`.

evidence_passages.text: Parsing lowercases the scheme: in `scheme start state` and `scheme state`, ASCII letters are appended to the buffer lowercased. For an HTTPS URL, that means `HTTPS:` becomes `https:`. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

claims.text: For `https`, the default port is `443`; if parsing reads port `443`, the URL record's port is set to `null`, and serialization omits the port.
acceptable_patterns: port is emitted only if it is non-null|serialization omits the port

evidence_passages.text: `https` is a special scheme whose default port is `443`. In `port state`, if the parsed port equals the scheme’s default port, the URL record’s `port` is set to `null`; in serialization, a port is emitted only if it is non-null. So `:443` is normalized away in the parsed URL record and disappears on serialization. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

claims.text: Dot segments are normalized during path parsing: `.` and ASCII-case-insensitive `%2e` are treated as single-dot segments, while `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, and `%2e%2e` trigger path shortening by removing the last path segment.
acceptable_patterns: shorten url'?s path|removes? the last path segment

evidence_passages.text: Dot segments are normalized during path parsing. A single-dot path segment is `.` or an ASCII-case-insensitive match for `%2e`. A double-dot path segment is `..`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, or `%2e%2e` with ASCII-case-insensitive matching. In `path state`, a double-dot segment triggers “shorten url’s path”, which removes the last path segment; the spec’s note says `/usr/..` becomes `/`. Single-dot segments are omitted from the path, except that the algorithm may append an empty segment when needed at the end. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

claims.text: When the parser encounters `#`, it starts fragment parsing, and fragment code points are UTF-8 percent-encoded using the fragment percent-encode set; because that set includes all code points above `U+007E`, non-ASCII fragment characters are percent-encoded.
acceptable_patterns: sees `?#`|encounters `?#`|starts fragment parsing when it sees `?#`
code points above `?U\+007E`?.+percent-encoded|non-ASCII fragment characters are percent-encoded

evidence_passages.text: The parser starts fragment parsing when it sees `#`. In `fragment state`, each fragment code point is UTF-8 percent-encoded with the fragment percent-encode set. That set includes the C0 control percent-encode set plus space, `"`, `<`, `>`, and `` ` ``; the C0 control percent-encode set includes all code points above `U+007E`, so non-ASCII fragment characters are percent-encoded too. (https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

rejected_claims.text: All already-valid percent-encoded path bytes are preserved exactly as-is during parsing, rather than ever being decoded.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence labels this as an inference and says the strongest support is algorithmic inference rather than a direct explicit rule.

rejected_claims.text: Parsing canonicalizes the hex digits of existing path percent-escapes to uppercase.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence says this is only an inference and not an explicit normative statement.

rejected_claims.text: Existing valid percent-encoded bytes in fragments are preserved unchanged during parsing.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence presents this only as an inference, not a directly supported fact.

rejected_claims.text: The current WHATWG URL Standard applies NFC normalization to Unicode hostnames during parsing.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence here does not directly quote or support NFC normalization as a performed step.

rejected_claims.text: Parsing removes a trailing dot from hostnames such as `example.com.`.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence does not support this claim.

rejected_claims.text: When parsing an HTTPS URL with a non-opaque Unicode hostname, the host is percent-decoded, UTF-8 decoded, and then run through the domain parser using Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing, yielding an ASCII IDNA form such as `xn--53h.example` or `xn--fa-hia.example` rather than raw Unicode in serialized output.
rejected_claims.reason: Le mécanisme général (percent-decoding, décodage UTF-8, domain parser / Unicode IDNA) est étayé par les extraits récupérés, mais la claim s'appuie sur des éléments non vérifiables dans les preuves : la source https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr46/tr46-35.html est une URL versionnée n'apparaissant que dans la réponse auto-citée de Codex (aucun payload d'outil, aucune page ouverte), et les exemples `xn--53h.example` / `xn--fa-hia.example` ne figurent dans aucun extrait réellement récupéré. De plus, l'un des acceptable_patterns exige littéralement ces exemples, ce qui constitue un motif de notation trop étroit : une réponse correcte à la question posée n'a pas à citer ces cas particuliers.

rejected_claims.text: For path parsing, non-separator path code points are UTF-8 percent-encoded with the path percent-encode set, and the cited parsed-components example shows `%20` remaining percent-encoded in a stored path segment rather than being decoded to a space.
rejected_claims.reason: L'exemple `file:///ada/Analytical%20Engine/README.md` et la « parsed-components table » ne sont corroborés par aucun extrait de page effectivement récupéré ; l'exemple porte en outre sur le schéma `file:` et non sur une URL HTTPS. L'extrait réellement récupéré du path state indique l'usage du fragment percent-encode set, ce qui entre en tension avec la formulation de la claim. Enfin, le volet « %20 reste encodé plutôt que décodé » relève de l'inférence explicitement signalée comme non explicitement normative dans les preuves, et recoupe une affirmation déjà présente dans rejected_claims. Le pattern requis dépend de l'exemple non vérifié, donc trop étroit.
